title: The Identity Theorem, the Maximum Principle and the Open Mapping Theorem

items.title: Locally injective holomorphic maps
Biholomorphic maps between complex domains
The locally zero locus of a holomorphic function is clopen
items.strategy: For a holomorphic function h on an open set, let L be the set of points having a neighbourhood on which h vanishes. It is open by definition. If a point b is not in L, the published zero-order factorization gives either h(b) nonzero or a finite-order isolated zero; after shrinking, no point near b can belong to L. Thus the complement is open and L is closed. Treat an empty open set and the identically zero function explicitly.

items.title: Identity theorem for holomorphic functions
items.strategy: Apply the argument to h=f-g. At an accumulation point a of the agreement set, finite-order factorization would make a an isolated zero, so h must vanish on a neighbourhood of a. The locally zero locus is therefore nonempty and is clopen by the preceding lemma; connectedness of the domain makes it the whole domain. Keep the hypothesis that the accumulation point belongs to the domain and handle f=g from the outset.

items.title: Zeros of a nonzero holomorphic function are isolated
items.strategy: Let f be holomorphic on a domain and not identically zero. At a zero a, the infinite-order alternative in the published factorization would make f vanish near a and then the identity theorem would make f identically zero. Hence the order is finite, and the nonvanishing factor in the local factorization makes a the only zero in a smaller disc.

items.title: Local degree of a nonconstant holomorphic map
The ring of holomorphic functions on a complex domain is an integral domain
items.strategy: Pointwise addition and multiplication make the holomorphic functions a commutative subring of the full complex function ring. If fg is the zero function and f is not the zero function, choose a point where f is nonzero; continuity makes f nonzero on a neighbourhood, so g vanishes there, and the identity theorem makes g the zero function. Nonemptiness of the domain and 0 not equal to 1 in the complex field separate the zero and unit functions.

items.title: A nonvanishing holomorphic function on a disc has a holomorphic logarithm
items.strategy: For nonvanishing h on a disc, h'/h is holomorphic and has a primitive H because the disc is star-shaped. Normalize H at the centre. The derivative of h exp(-H) is zero, so it is the constant h(a). Choose a scalar logarithm c of h(a); then L=H+c is holomorphic and exp L=h. Check that the disc is nonempty, its radius is positive, and every denominator is nonzero.

items.title: Holomorphic roots of a nonvanishing function on a disc
items.strategy: For a positive natural m, take a holomorphic logarithm L of h and define q=exp(L/m). The complex exponential addition law gives q^m=h. To impose a chosen root value at the centre, normalize the logarithm by a constant whose exponential is that chosen scalar. Treat m=1 and record that m=0 is excluded before division.

items.title: A nonzero complex derivative gives a local biholomorphism
items.strategy: View the holomorphic map as a smooth map between real coordinate planes. Its real Jacobian determinant is |f'(a)|^2, hence is nonzero. Apply the Euclidean inverse function theorem to obtain a local C1 inverse. The real derivative of that inverse is the inverse of multiplication by f', hence is again complex-linear; the real-linearity and Cauchy-Riemann equivalence makes the inverse holomorphic, with derivative 1/f'.

items.title: Local normal form of a nonconstant holomorphic map
items.strategy: Let m be the local degree at a. Factor f(z)-f(a)=(z-a)^m h(z) with h(a) nonzero, shrink to a disc on which h never vanishes, and take a holomorphic mth root q of h. Put phi(z)=(z-a)q(z). Then phi(a)=0 and phi'(a)=q(a) is nonzero, so the preceding lemma makes phi biholomorphic after shrinking once more, while f(z)-f(a)=phi(z)^m on that neighbourhood.

items.title: A local degree-m holomorphic map has m nearby sheets
items.strategy: Given any neighbourhood N of a, intersect it with the source of the local coordinate phi from the normal-form theorem and choose a positive radius r whose disc lies in the resulting open image. Restrict the source to phi^{-1}(D(0,r)), which now lies inside N. The mth-power map carries D(0,r) onto D(0,r^m); the centre has one preimage of multiplicity m, while every noncentral value has exactly m distinct roots and therefore exactly m distinct source preimages. Include m=1 and exclude m=0 through the local-degree definition.

items.title: Open mapping theorem for holomorphic functions
items.strategy: Let f be nonconstant on a complex domain and O an open subset of its domain. At each a in O, the identity theorem rules out local constancy and the local normal form supplies a source neighbourhood whose image contains a disc about f(a). Thus every point of f[O] is interior, so f[O] is open. Handle O empty separately and do not use Rouché's theorem or the argument principle.

items.title: Complex-analytic and Banach-space open mapping theorems
Local maximum modulus principle
items.strategy: If a nonconstant holomorphic f had a local maximum of |f| at a, the open mapping theorem would make the image of a sufficiently small neighbourhood an open set containing f(a). Every complex neighbourhood of f(a) contains a point of modulus strictly larger than |f(a)|, a contradiction. Include f(a)=0 and constant functions explicitly.

items.title: Maximum principle for the real part of a holomorphic function
items.strategy: If Re f has a local maximum at a and f is nonconstant, the open image of a small neighbourhood of a contains f(a)+epsilon for some positive real epsilon, whose real part is larger. This contradiction makes f constant. The Statement keeps only the real-part form.

items.title: Boundary maximum modulus principle on a bounded domain
items.strategy: For a nonempty bounded complex domain Omega and f continuous on its closure and holomorphic inside, Heine-Borel makes the closure compact and the extreme value theorem gives a maximizer of |f|. An interior maximizer makes f constant by the local principle; continuity on the closure then gives the same value on the nonempty boundary. Otherwise a maximizer already lies on the boundary. Check the constant case and boundary nonemptiness.

items.title: Maximum modulus principle with boundary and infinity control
items.strategy: Assume |f| approaches at most M at every finite boundary point and, when the domain is unbounded, outside sufficiently large discs, using an epsilon-neighbourhood formulation. For epsilon>0 the set K={z:|f(z)|>=M+epsilon} is bounded, closed in the plane, and disjoint from the boundary, hence compactly contained in the domain. If K were nonempty, |f| would attain an interior maximum there and the local maximum principle would make f constant, contradicting the boundary or infinity control. Let epsilon decrease to zero and treat the whole-plane domain through the infinity clause.

items.title: Minimum modulus principle for a nowhere-zero holomorphic function
items.strategy: If f is nowhere zero and |f| has a local minimum, then 1/f is holomorphic and its modulus has a local maximum at the same point. The local maximum modulus principle makes 1/f constant, hence f constant. Keep the nonvanishing hypothesis explicit and include constant nonzero functions.

items.title: Constant boundary modulus forces an interior zero or constancy
items.strategy: Let |f| equal M on the boundary of a bounded domain. If M=0, the boundary maximum principle gives f=0. If M>0 and f has no zero, apply the boundary maximum principle to f and to 1/f to get |f|<=M and |f|>=M throughout. Then |f| has an interior local maximum, so f is constant. The only remaining nonconstant case has an interior zero.

items.title: Maximum principle on a closed strip for bounded holomorphic functions
items.strategy: On the strip 0<=Re z<=1, let g be bounded, continuous on the closed strip, holomorphic inside, and have boundary modulus at most one. For epsilon>0 multiply by exp(epsilon(z^2-1)). Its modulus stays at most one on the vertical boundary and decays on high horizontal lines. Choose a large rectangle, apply the bounded-domain boundary maximum theorem, then let the rectangle contain an arbitrary fixed point and send epsilon to zero. Treat g=0 and points on both boundary lines.

items.title: Hadamard three-lines theorem
items.strategy: For bounded f on the closed strip, let M(x)=sup_y |f(x+iy)|. For delta>0 normalize by G_delta(z)=f(z)(M(0)+delta)^(z-1)(M(1)+delta)^(-z), defining positive-base complex powers through exp(z log a). Its modulus is at most one on both vertical boundaries, so the strip lemma bounds it inside. Rearrange and let delta decrease to zero, including a zero boundary supremum. Applying the same estimate after an affine rescaling of any substrip gives log-convexity of M and includes both endpoints.

items.title: Hadamard three-lines and complex interpolation
Holomorphic inverse function theorem and local-degree criterion
items.strategy: For a nonconstant holomorphic f on a domain, prove equivalence of f'(a) nonzero, local degree one, local injectivity, and local biholomorphy. Factorization identifies degree one with a nonzero derivative. The local-biholomorphism lemma proves sufficiency, while local biholomorphy implies local injectivity. If a locally injective map had degree m>1, the local multiplicity theorem would give m distinct nearby preimages, a contradiction. Differentiate the two inverse identities to obtain the reciprocal derivative formula.

items.title: An injective holomorphic map has no critical point and is biholomorphic onto its image
items.strategy: An injective holomorphic map on a complex domain is nonconstant and locally injective at every point, so the inverse theorem makes its derivative nonzero everywhere and gives holomorphic local inverses. The open mapping theorem makes the image open. The global set-theoretic inverse agrees with each local inverse, so it is holomorphic throughout the image and the original map is biholomorphic onto that image.

title: The Identity Theorem, the Maximum Principle and the Open Mapping Theorem — Examples

items.title: The complex Pythagorean identity by the identity theorem
items.strategy: The entire functions h(z)=sin(z)^2+cos(z)^2 and the constant one agree for every real z by the published real trigonometric identity. The real axis has an accumulation point in the complex plane, so the identity theorem gives h=1 on all of C. This is a genuinely different proof from expanding the published complex addition formulas; cross-reference that route without using it in this proof.

items.title: The local mapping of complex squaring at zero and at one
items.strategy: For f(z)=z^2, the order of f(z)-f(0) at zero is two, so the local degree is two and every sufficiently small nonzero value has two local preimages. At one, f(z)-f(1)=(z-1)(z+1) has a nonvanishing factor at one, so the local degree is one and f is biholomorphic on a sufficiently small neighbourhood. Give explicit square-root preimages near zero and an explicit disc around one avoiding the collision z and -z.

items.title: An exact polynomial bound from the boundary maximum principle
items.strategy: For p(z)=z^2-2z+2 on the closed unit disc, the triangle inequality gives |p(z)|<=5. Equality holds at z=-1, a boundary point, where p(-1)=5. The boundary maximum principle shows there is no hidden larger interior value, so the exact maximum is five. Verify the polynomial is holomorphic and the witness belongs to the boundary.

items.title: Agreement accumulating only at the boundary does not force a holomorphic identity
items.strategy: On the punctured plane take f(z)=sin(1/z) and g=0. Both are holomorphic, and f vanishes at 1/(k pi) for every nonzero integer k; these distinct points converge to zero. Yet zero is not in the domain and f is not the zero function, for example at a point whose reciprocal is pi/2. Verify the punctured plane is a complex domain and every displayed point lies in it.

items.title: A flat smooth real function has no holomorphic extension near zero
items.strategy: Define psi(0)=0 and psi(x)=exp(-1/x^2) for nonzero x. Away from zero, induction with the product and chain rules writes every derivative as a polynomial in 1/x times exp(-1/x^2). Exponential domination makes these expressions and the required difference quotients tend to zero at zero, so every derivative extends there with value zero and psi is smooth; exponential positivity gives psi(x)>0 off zero. If a holomorphic function near zero restricted to psi on a real interval, restriction to the real axis would make every complex derivative at zero vanish. The coefficient formula and Taylor expansion would then make the extension zero near zero, contradicting the positive real values. Check both sides of zero explicitly.

items.title: A nonconstant Blaschke factor has constant boundary modulus
items.strategy: Fix a in the open unit disc and use B_a(z)=(z-a)/(1-conjugate(a)z). Its pole lies outside the closed unit disc, it is holomorphic on a neighbourhood of that disc, and direct expansion gives |z-a|=|1-conjugate(a)z| when |z|=1. Thus |B_a|=1 on the boundary while B_a(a)=0, so it is nonconstant and realizes the zero alternative in the constant-boundary-modulus corollary. Include a=0 and general a.

items.title: FALSE: the local maximum modulus principle needs no connectedness
items.strategy: Take the union of two disjoint open discs and define f to be zero on one component and one on the other. The function is holomorphic because it is locally constant. Its modulus has a local maximum at every point of the second component, but f is not constant on the whole open set. This isolates connectedness as the missing hypothesis without weakening the valid theorem on a domain.

items.title: FALSE: every interior local modulus minimum forces constancy
items.strategy: On the unit disc the identity function f(z)=z is holomorphic and nonconstant, while |f| has its global minimum zero at the interior point zero. The valid minimum modulus theorem does not apply because f vanishes there. Verify both the minimum and nonconstancy directly.

items.title: FALSE: every injective real-differentiable planar map has nonzero Jacobian
items.strategy: Use F(x,y)=(x^3,y). The factorization x^3-u^3=(x-u)((x+u/2)^2+3u^2/4) proves injectivity on the whole real plane, and the derivative matrix is diag(3x^2,1), whose determinant is zero on the vertical axis. This contrasts with injective holomorphic maps, whose derivatives cannot vanish, and it does not claim that the real inverse is differentiable at those points.

items.title: FALSE: boundary control alone gives the maximum principle on an unbounded domain
items.strategy: On the upper half-plane take f(z)=exp(-iz). It is holomorphic and continuous on the closed half-plane, and its modulus is one on the real boundary. For z=x+iy with y>0 its modulus is exp(y), which is unbounded. Thus the bounded-domain conclusion fails without the additional control at infinity stated in the preceding theorem.
